title: Our solar system
introduction: You already know Earth travels around the Sun.
But Earth has neighbours, and the Sun has a whole family.
We will meet its eight planets and some smaller travellers.
We will discover what makes them part of one solar system.

steps.title: The Sun’s family
paragraphs: Our solar system includes the Sun, planets, moons, and many smaller objects.
Gravity is the pull that objects have on one another.
The Sun’s gravity helps keep the planets travelling around it.
These objects form a connected family in space.

steps.title: One star, many planets
paragraphs: The Sun is our solar system’s only star.
It makes the light reaching its planets.
Planets move around the Sun, but they are not stars.
We usually see planets because they reflect sunlight.

steps.title: The eight in order
paragraphs: First come Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Then come Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
This order describes their paths around the Sun.
It does not mean they stand in one straight line.
steps.glaux: An order map is not a picture of tonight.

steps.title: The four rocky worlds
paragraphs: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the inner planets.
Scientists also call them rocky planets.
They have solid, rocky surfaces.
They still look different from one another.
Earth’s oceans are visible from space. Mars looks reddish in many images.

steps.title: The four giant worlds
paragraphs: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are the outer planets.
All four are giant planets with deep layers of gases.
They lack solid ground like the surface of Earth.
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.
Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
These names describe different materials inside, not icy ground to walk on.

steps.title: Different faces of giant planets
paragraphs: Jupiter shows wide bands of clouds.
Saturn’s rings contain mostly icy pieces.
Uranus and Neptune look bluish in many pictures.
Scientists sometimes adjust pictures to reveal details. These are called processed images.
A picture may not show natural colours exactly.
steps.glaux: An image is evidence. Its colours can also tell a story.

steps.title: Other planets have moons
paragraphs: Earth’s Moon is not alone.
Many other planets have natural satellites, also called moons.
Mercury and Venus have none.
These moons orbit their planets. Those planets travel around the Sun.
The moons still belong to our solar system.

steps.title: Small travellers
paragraphs: The solar system contains smaller travellers, too.
Asteroids are mainly rocky objects orbiting the Sun.
Comets contain ice, dust, and rock. They also orbit the Sun.
Some comets form bright tails when they approach the Sun.
Their tails generally point away from the Sun.
steps.glaux: Not every traveller is a planet.

steps.title: Pluto still belongs
paragraphs: Pluto belongs to our solar system.
It is a dwarf planet, rather than one of the eight planets.
Dwarf planets orbit the Sun and are nearly round.
Scientists use more than shape to decide these groups.
steps.glaux: A different name does not mean a world has disappeared.

steps.title: Our little neighbourhood
paragraphs: Our solar system has one star: the Sun.
Eight planets orbit it in a known order.
Four are rocky worlds; four are giant worlds.
Many planets have moons.
Asteroids, comets, and dwarf planets belong here too.
steps.glaux: One star, many worlds. Keep their connections in mind.

glossary.definition: The Sun and the objects connected to it by gravity.
glossary.example: Earth belongs to our solar system.

glossary.definition: The pull that objects have on one another.
glossary.example: Gravity pulls a dropped ball towards Earth.

glossary.definition: A very hot object in space that produces its own light.
Large, nearly round worlds that orbit a star. Scientists also use other classification rules.
The path an object follows around another in space.
glossary.example: Mars follows an orbit around the Sun.

glossary.definition: The first four planets from our Sun.
Giant planets made mostly of two light gases: hydrogen and helium.
glossary.example: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.

glossary.definition: Giant planets with a greater share of heavier materials inside than gas giants.
glossary.example: Uranus is an ice giant. This does not mean icy ground.

glossary.definition: Bands of many small pieces travelling around a planet.
Pictures adjusted or combined to make details easier to see.
glossary.example: A planet picture may use adjusted colours.

glossary.definition: Objects not built by people that orbit larger objects in space.
glossary.example: Our Moon is Earth’s natural satellite.

glossary.definition: Relatively small, mainly rocky bodies travelling around the Sun.
Small bodies containing ice, dust and rock that travel around the Sun.
glossary.example: Some comets develop bright tails near the Sun.

glossary.definition: A nearly round world orbiting the Sun, in a different group from the eight planets.

orderPractice.prompt: Place the four inner planets in order, moving away from the Sun.
orderPractice.reference: Use the atlas above. This is practice, not a memory test.
orderPractice.hint: Start with Mercury. Earth is third, between Venus and Mars.
orderPractice.right: Yes. Mercury, Venus, Earth, then Mars. You have followed the inner planets outward.
feedback: Mercury is first. Start at the Sun and follow the numbered atlas.
Venus comes after Mercury, before Earth.
Earth is third, between Venus and Mars.

sorting.prompt: Choose the best group for each object.
sorting.hint: Ask what each object is. A moon belongs here even though it orbits a planet.
sorting.right: You sorted the objects by what they are, not just how they look.

cards.title: Sun
cards.feedback: The Sun produces its own light. It is our solar system’s star.

cards.title: Mars
cards.feedback: Mars is the fourth planet orbiting the Sun.

cards.title: Saturn
cards.feedback: Saturn is a planet. Its rings do not make it a star.

cards.title: Earth’s Moon
cards.feedback: Our Moon orbits Earth. It is Earth’s natural satellite.

cards.title: Asteroid
cards.feedback: An asteroid is a small, mainly rocky body. Orbiting the Sun alone does not make a planet.

cards.title: Comet
cards.feedback: A comet is a small body containing ice, dust and rock. It does not produce sunlight.

cards.title: Pluto
cards.feedback: Pluto is a dwarf planet. It still belongs to our solar system.

plutoDetail: Astronomers also consider whether a world dominates its orbital region through gravity.
Pluto has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood: the region around its path.
“Cleared” does not mean a planet’s path is completely empty.
